explicit_validation.explanation: The paper explicitly validates LLM-as-a-judge against human evaluation by comparing agreement using Krippendorff's alpha and analyzing citation recovery performance metrics (precision, recall, F1)

prompts.notes: Full prompt example provided in appendix Table 15 shows exact zero-shot instruction with example

inter_annotator_agreement.value: Not specified numerically in text (values discussed in context)
inter_annotator_agreement.interpretation: moderate to good agreement for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5

guidelines.notes: Full annotation guidelines and interface details provided in Appendix F with multiple examples

sample_size.notes: Evaluation uses all 100 instances, with two settings: sample (one evidence passage per claim) and full (all evidence passages per claim)

quantitative_scores.value: Higher for LLM annotators than NLI annotators
quantitative_scores.notes: LLM annotators have much higher correlation with human annotators than NLI annotators
Best attribution performance with machine-selected evidence

validation_results.summary_finding: LLM-based annotations have stronger correlation with human annotations compared to NLI models, with GPT-4 showing the best alignment as an automatic annotator.

criteria_mapping.notes: Both LLM and human evaluate citation recovery and evidence attribution, while only human evaluates utility/helpfulness using sliding scale assessment
